title: Count Primes Up to N
description:
Count how many prime numbers are less than or equal to n. A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes; checking each number by trial division is too slow for the largest inputs.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 106

Input

A single integer n.

Output

A single integer: the number of primes p with p ≤ n.

Example

Input:

10

Output:

4

The primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7.

title: Prime Factorization
description:
Write the prime factorization of a positive integer n.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 1010

Input

A single integer n.

Output

Print the prime factors in increasing order, separated by * (a space, an asterisk, a space). A prime p that appears e > 1 times is written as p^e; a prime that appears once is written as just p. If n = 1, print 1.

Example

Input:

360

Output:

2^3 * 3^2 * 5

title: Sum of All Divisors
description:
Let σ(n) be the sum of all positive divisors of n, including 1 and n itself. Compute σ(n). Looping over every number from 1 to n is far too slow; factor n and use the formula σ(pe) = 1 + p + p2 + ... + pe, which is multiplicative over distinct primes.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 1011

Input

A single integer n.

Output

A single integer σ(n).

Example

Input:

12

Output:

28

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 12 = 28.
solution:
n = int(input())
res = 1
p = 2
while p * p <= n:
    if n % p == 0:
        term = 1
        pk = 1
        while n % p == 0:
            n //= p
            pk *= p
            term += pk
        res *= term
    p += 1 if p == 2 else 2
if n > 1:
    res *= 1 + n
print(res)

title: Perfect, Abundant or Deficient
description:
The proper divisors of n are its positive divisors other than n itself. Let s be their sum. Then n is:

  • Perfect if s = n
  • Abundant if s > n
  • Deficient if s < n

Note that 1 has no proper divisors, so s = 0 and 1 is deficient.

Constraints: 1 ≤ T ≤ 100, 1 ≤ n ≤ 106

Input

The first line contains T. Each of the next T lines contains one integer n.

Output

For each n, in input order, print a line n: Kind where Kind is Perfect, Abundant or Deficient.

Example

Input:

3
6
12
7

Output:

6: Perfect
12: Abundant
7: Deficient
solution:
t = int(input())
for _ in range(t):
    n = int(input())
    s = 0
    i = 1
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            s += i
            j = n // i
            if j != i:
                s += j
        i += 1
    s -= n
    kind = "Perfect" if s == n else ("Abundant" if s > n else "Deficient")
    print(f"{n}: {kind}")

title: Fast Modular Exponentiation
description:
Compute ab mod m. Because b can be as large as 1018, you must use exponentiation by squaring (binary exponentiation) instead of multiplying a by itself b times. By definition a0 = 1 (including 00 = 1).

Constraints: 0 ≤ a, b ≤ 1018, 1 ≤ m ≤ 109

Input

One line with three integers a b m.

Output

A single integer: ab mod m, a value in the range 0 to m - 1.

Example

Input:

2 10 1000

Output:

24

210 = 1024, and 1024 mod 1000 = 24.
solution:
a, b, m = map(int, input().split())
res = 1 % m
a %= m
while b > 0:
    if b & 1:
        res = res * a % m
    a = a * a % m
    b >>= 1
print(res)

title: Binomial Coefficients Modulo a Prime
description:
Answer Q queries. Each query gives n and r; print C(n, r) mod 1000000007, the number of ways to choose r items from n, reduced modulo the prime 109 + 7. If r < 0 or r > n, the answer is 0.

Hint: precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 109 + 7 once (using Fermat's little theorem for the inverse), then answer each query in O(1).

Constraints: 1 ≤ Q ≤ 1000, 0 ≤ n ≤ 105, -10 ≤ r ≤ n + 10

Input

The first line contains Q. Each of the next Q lines contains two integers n r.

Output

For each query, in order, print the answer on its own line.

Example

Input:

3
5 2
10 0
4 7

Output:

10
1
0
solution:
MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
q = int(input())
qs = [tuple(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]
N = max(n for n, r in qs) + 1
fact = [1] * (N + 1)
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
inv = [1] * (N + 1)
inv[N] = pow(fact[N], MOD - 2, MOD)
for i in range(N, 0, -1):
    inv[i - 1] = inv[i] * i % MOD
out = []
for n, r in qs:
    if r < 0 or r > n:
        out.append(0)
    else:
        out.append(fact[n] * inv[r] % MOD * inv[n - r] % MOD)
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))

title: Fibonacci Modulo for Huge N
description:
The Fibonacci numbers are F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, and F(k) = F(k-1) + F(k-2). Answer Q queries, each asking for F(n) mod m.

With n up to 1018, a loop is impossible. Use the fast doubling identities, which compute F(n) in O(log n) steps:

  • F(2k) = F(k) · (2·F(k+1) − F(k))
  • F(2k+1) = F(k)2 + F(k+1)2

Be careful to keep every intermediate value non-negative and reduced modulo m. When m = 1 every answer is 0.

Constraints: 1 ≤ Q ≤ 500, 0 ≤ n ≤ 1018, 1 ≤ m ≤ 109

Input

The first line contains Q. Each of the next Q lines contains two integers n m.

Output

For each query, in order, print F(n) mod m on its own line.

Example

Input:

3
10 1000
0 7
100 1000000007

Output:

55
0
687995182
solution:
import sys

def fib(n, m):
    a, b = 0, 1 % m
    for bit in bin(n)[2:]:
        c = a * ((2 * b - a) % m) % m
        d = (a * a + b * b) % m
        if bit == '1':
            a, b = d, (c + d) % m
        else:
            a, b = c, d
    return a

q = int(input())
out = []
for _ in range(q):
    n, m = map(int, input().split())
    out.append(fib(n, m) % m)
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))

title: Euler's Totient Function
description:
Euler's totient φ(n) counts the integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n and gcd(k, n) = 1. Compute it using the product formula φ(n) = n · ∏ (1 − 1/p) over the distinct primes p dividing n, using only integer arithmetic. By definition φ(1) = 1.

Constraints: 1 ≤ T ≤ 20, 1 ≤ n ≤ 109

Input

The first line contains T. Each of the next T lines contains one integer n.

Output

For each n, in order, print φ(n) on its own line.

Example

Input:

3
9
10
13

Output:

6
4
12

title: Trailing Zeros of a Factorial
description:
Count the number of trailing zeros in the decimal representation of n!. Do not compute n! itself. Each trailing zero comes from a factor of 10 = 2 × 5, and factors of 5 are the scarcer ones, so the answer is ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + .... Note that 0! = 1 has no trailing zeros.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 1018

Input

A single integer n.

Output

A single integer: the number of trailing zeros of n!.

Example

Input:

25

Output:

6
solution:
n = int(input())
c = 0
p = 5
while p <= n:
    c += n // p
    p *= 5
print(c)

title: Longest Collatz Chain
description:
The Collatz sequence starting at x repeatedly applies: if x is even, x → x/2; otherwise x → 3x + 1, stopping when it reaches 1. The chain length is the number of terms, including the start and the final 1 (so the chain length of 1 is 1, and of 6 it is 9: 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1).

Among all starting values 1 ≤ x ≤ N, find the one with the longest chain. If several share the longest length, choose the smallest such x. Store (memoize) lengths you have already computed; recomputing every chain from scratch is too slow.

Constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 105

Input

A single integer N.

Output

Two integers separated by one space: the best starting value and its chain length.

Example

Input:

10

Output:

9 20
solution:
N = int(input())
cache = [0] * (N + 1)
cache[1] = 1
best, bl = 1, 1
for s in range(2, N + 1):
    x = s
    path = []
    while x > N or cache[x] == 0:
        path.append(x)
        x = x // 2 if x % 2 == 0 else 3 * x + 1
    L = cache[x]
    for y in reversed(path):
        L += 1
        if y <= N:
            cache[y] = L
    if cache[s] > bl:
        best, bl = s, cache[s]
print(best, bl)

title: Convert Between Any Two Bases
description:
Convert a non-negative number written in base B1 into base B2. Digits beyond 9 are the uppercase letters A = 10, B = 11, ..., Z = 35. Lowercase letters never appear in the input. The input number may have leading zeros, and it can be up to 40 digits long, which is larger than a 64-bit integer.

Constraints: 2 ≤ B1, B2 ≤ 36; every digit of the number is valid in base B1.

Input

The first line contains two integers B1 B2. The second line contains the number in base B1.

Output

The same value written in base B2, using uppercase letters for digits above 9 and no leading zeros. Zero is printed as 0.

Example

Input:

16 2
FF

Output:

11111111
solution:
b1, b2 = map(int, input().split())
s = input().strip()
D = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
v = 0
for ch in s:
    v = v * b1 + D.index(ch)
if v == 0:
    print(0)
else:
    out = []
    while v:
        v, r = divmod(v, b2)
        out.append(D[r])
    print("".join(reversed(out)))

title: Happy Numbers
description:
Start with a positive integer and repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. If the process eventually reaches 1, the number is happy. Otherwise it loops forever in a cycle that never contains 1, and the number is unhappy. For example, 19 → 82 → 68 → 100 → 1, so 19 is happy. Detect the cycle (for example with a set of numbers already seen) instead of looping forever.

Constraints: 1 ≤ T ≤ 100, 1 ≤ n ≤ 1018

Input

The first line contains T. Each of the next T lines contains one integer n.

Output

For each n, in order, print Happy or Not Happy on its own line.

Example

Input:

3
19
2
7

Output:

Happy
Not Happy
Happy
solution:
t = int(input())
for _ in range(t):
    n = int(input())
    seen = set()
    while n != 1 and n not in seen:
        seen.add(n)
        n = sum(int(d) ** 2 for d in str(n))
    print("Happy" if n == 1 else "Not Happy")

title: N-th Ugly Number
description:
An ugly number is a positive integer whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5. By convention 1 is the first ugly number, so the sequence begins 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, ... Find the n-th ugly number (1-based).

Testing each integer in turn is far too slow, because ugly numbers become very sparse. Build the sequence in order instead, with three pointers (one each for multiplying by 2, 3 and 5).

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 105

Input

A single integer n.

Output

The n-th ugly number. It can exceed 64 bits for the largest n.

Example

Input:

10

Output:

12
solution:
n = int(input())
u = [1] * n
i2 = i3 = i5 = 0
for k in range(1, n):
    a, b, c = u[i2] * 2, u[i3] * 3, u[i5] * 5
    v = min(a, b, c)
    u[k] = v
    if v == a:
        i2 += 1
    if v == b:
        i3 += 1
    if v == c:
        i5 += 1
print(u[n - 1])

title: Catalan Numbers Modulo a Prime
description:
The Catalan numbers are C0 = 1, C1 = 1, C2 = 2, C3 = 5, C4 = 14, ..., given by the closed form Cn = (2n)! / ((n+1)! · n!). Answer Q queries, each asking for Cn mod 1000000007.

The O(n2) recurrence is too slow for large n. Precompute factorials modulo the prime, and divide using modular inverses.

Constraints: 1 ≤ Q ≤ 1000, 0 ≤ n ≤ 105

Input

The first line contains Q. Each of the next Q lines contains one integer n.

Output

For each query, in order, print Cn mod 1000000007 on its own line.

Example

Input:

4
0
3
4
10

Output:

1
5
14
16796
solution:
MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
q = int(input())
ns = [int(input()) for _ in range(q)]
N = 2 * max(ns) + 2
fact = [1] * (N + 1)
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
out = []
for n in ns:
    out.append(fact[2 * n] * pow(fact[n + 1] * fact[n] % MOD, MOD - 2, MOD) % MOD)
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))

title: Fewest Perfect Squares
description:
Find the minimum number of perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, ...) that sum to n. A square may be used more than once. For example, 12 = 4 + 4 + 4 needs 3 squares and 13 = 4 + 9 needs 2.

With n up to 1011, the usual dynamic programming solution is far too slow. Use number theory instead:

  • The answer is always at most 4 (Lagrange's four-square theorem).
  • It is exactly 4 if and only if n = 4a(8b + 7) (Legendre's three-square theorem).
  • It is at most 2 if and only if every prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) appears with an even exponent in the factorization of n.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 1011

Input

A single integer n.

Output

A single integer from 1 to 4.

Example

Input:

12

Output:

3

title: Integer Square Root of a Big Number
description:
For each non-negative integer n, print ⌊√n⌋, the largest integer r with r2 ≤ n. The numbers can have up to 60 digits, so floating-point n ** 0.5 gives wrong answers. Do not use math.isqrt or math.sqrt. Use integer binary search or Newton's method.

Constraints: 1 ≤ T ≤ 50, 0 ≤ n < 1060

Input

The first line contains T. Each of the next T lines contains one integer n.

Output

For each n, in order, print ⌊√n⌋ on its own line.

Example

Input:

3
17
16
0

Output:

4
4
0

title: Fraction to Recurring Decimal
description:
Given a numerator and a denominator, write the fraction as a decimal. If the fractional part repeats, enclose the shortest repeating block in parentheses, placed as early as possible. For example, 1/6 = 0.1(6) and 1/3 = 0.(3).

  • If the result is an integer, print it with no decimal point (for example 4).
  • A terminating decimal is printed in full with no trailing zeros (for example -2.5).
  • Print a leading - only if the value is negative. Zero is printed as 0.
  • The integer part is always printed, so values between -1 and 1 start with 0. or -0..

Track the position at which each remainder first appeared during long division.

Constraints: -109 ≤ a ≤ 109, 1 ≤ |b| ≤ 2000

Input

One line with two integers a b (numerator and denominator).

Output

The decimal representation described above.

Example

Input:

1 6

Output:

0.1(6)

title: Modular Inverse via Extended GCD
description:
For each pair a m, find the modular inverse of a modulo m: the unique x with 0 ≤ x < m and a · x ≡ 1 (mod m). The inverse exists exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1. The modulus need not be prime, so Fermat's little theorem does not apply. Use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

Special case: when m = 1, every integer is congruent to 0, so the answer is 0.

Constraints: 1 ≤ Q ≤ 200, 0 ≤ a ≤ 1018, 1 ≤ m ≤ 1018

Input

The first line contains Q. Each of the next Q lines contains two integers a m.

Output

For each query, in order, print the inverse, or No inverse if it does not exist.

Example

Input:

3
3 11
10 17
6 9

Output:

4
12
No inverse

title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
description:
Find the smallest non-negative integer x satisfying all k congruences x ≡ ai (mod mi).

The moduli are not necessarily pairwise coprime. Merge the congruences one at a time. Two congruences x ≡ a1 (mod m1) and x ≡ a2 (mod m2) are compatible only when a1 ≡ a2 (mod gcd(m1, m2)), and they combine into a single congruence modulo lcm(m1, m2). Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to do the merge. Trying every candidate x is hopeless, because the lcm can be astronomically large.

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 60, 1 ≤ mi ≤ 109, 0 ≤ ai < mi

Input

The first line contains k. Each of the next k lines contains two integers ai mi.

Output

If a solution exists, print two integers separated by one space: the smallest non-negative solution x and L = lcm(m1, ..., mk). All solutions are then x + t·L. Otherwise print No solution.

Example

Input:

3
2 3
3 5
2 7

Output:

23 105
solution:
from math import gcd

def eg(a, b):
    x0, x1 = 1, 0
    while b:
        q = a // b
        a, b = b, a - q * b
        x0, x1 = x1, x0 - q * x1
    return a, x0

k = int(input())
x, L = 0, 1
ok = True
for _ in range(k):
    a, m = map(int, input().split())
    if not ok:
        continue
    g, p = eg(L % m, m)
    if (a - x) % g != 0:
        ok = False
        continue
    mg = m // g
    t = ((a - x) // g) * p % mg
    x = x + L * t
    L = L * mg
    x %= L
print(f"{x} {L}" if ok else "No solution")

title: Count Primes in a Huge Interval
description:
Count the primes p with L ≤ p ≤ R. The endpoints can be as large as 1012, so you cannot sieve up to R, and testing each number by trial division is too slow, since the interval can hold up to a million numbers.

Use a segmented sieve: first sieve the primes up to √R, then cross out their multiples inside [L, R] only. Remember that 1 is not prime, and that a base prime itself may lie inside the interval.

Constraints: 1 ≤ L ≤ R ≤ 1012, R − L ≤ 106

Input

One line with two integers L R.

Output

A single integer: the number of primes in [L, R].

Example

Input:

10 30

Output:

6

The primes are 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29.
